projects.title: Trading-research dashboard
projects.plain: A live mission-control screen for my research projects -- one glance from any device shows what every system is doing right now.
projects.summary: FastAPI + Jinja2 monitoring and decision-support dashboard for a personal quantitative-trading workflow. Surfaces include project tracking, an editorial organisation chart, a Phaser 3 isometric office-RPG view of active research agents, a live-demo strategy monitor with a tail-concentration auditor, and a Smart Money Radar that scores 13F / Form-4 / political-disclosure signals (1-100). Deployed via Tailscale Funnel to a Windows VPS with a hard-restart deploy script.
projects.deep_dive_intro: A FastAPI dashboard that surfaces the live state of a multi-strategy quantitative trading research workflow. Each page is a thin Jinja2 view over JSON state files that a separate baker process refreshes on a schedule; the server itself is read-only and never opens MT5, mutates state, or toggles halt files.
projects.architecture: FastAPI server on 127.0.0.1:8765 mounts one route per concern (hub, office, projects, anchor, portfolio, chat). Each route imports a small loader module (BOT/dashboard/*.py) that reads a JSON file under BOT/dashboard/data/, validates required keys, and returns a dict that the matching Jinja2 template renders. Tailscale Funnel exposes the bind publicly; a PowerShell deploy script enumerates the file list explicitly (no globs), scps each, and hard-restarts the Windows service. Authenticated /api/* routes use HTTP Basic, fail-closed when DASHBOARD_PASSWORD is unset; static + healthz stay public.
lessons: Server-side state baking beats live computation: a separate process refreshes JSON every cycle, so the request path stays under a few ms and survives broker outages without a runtime DB.
An explicit file list in the deploy script beats globs on Windows -- the same bug class (a new module silently not shipped) bit anchor.py, portfolio.py, and today.py before the rule was internalised.
Tests scale with surfaces: one pytest module per page, fail-closed 503 on schema invalidity, and an isolation guard that forbids public pages from linking to authenticated routes.

Two-stage subagent review caught defect classes that single-pass implementation missed: ZeroDivisionError on empty totals, BOM in PowerShell-written JSON, and $ErrorActionPreference=Stop aborting git on outside-repo globs.

projects.title: LINE Official Account bot
projects.plain: A chat assistant that never forgets: it lives in the LINE app, remembers everyone's plans, and sends the reminders all by itself.
projects.summary: Multi-owner LINE Messaging API bot with scheduled reminders, daily SQLite snapshots, Sunday digest, and pre-alert dedupe. Designed to run unattended on a Windows VPS with a self-healing restart loop.
projects.deep_dive_intro: A multi-owner LINE Official Account bot that holds a small social schedule, fires reminders ahead of deadlines, and issues a weekly digest -- with the operational discipline of a paid service even though it runs on a single Windows VPS.
projects.architecture: FastAPI webhook receives LINE Messaging API events; commands (/bind, /unbind, /list, /delete N, /retry) route into a SQLite store keyed by owner. A 60-second scheduler tick walks pending reminders, sends pre-alerts ~1 hour ahead on a dedicated thread with a prealert_sent_ts column to de-dupe, then the main reminder, then a Sunday digest. A nightly job runs SQLite's online backup API into logs/db_backup/bot-YYYY-MM-DD.db with a 7-day retention. A self-healing restart loop catches uncaught exceptions and brings the process back up.
lessons: De-dupe by timestamp column in the row, not by an in-memory set: process restarts must not double-fire a pre-alert the user already received.
Online SQLite backup (sqlite3.backup) survives a live writer; a naive file copy can race with the WAL and produce an unreadable snapshot.
Multi-owner before multi-tenant: a single SQLite file with an owner_id column shipped in days; a per-tenant database scheme would have shipped in months and not been any safer at this scale.

PowerShell 5.1 writes .ps1 files as LF unless you go through .NET WriteAllText with UTF8Encoding(false) -- the parser then chokes on multi-line here-strings during deploys. Learned the hard way mid-deploy.

projects.title: Quantitative trading research framework
projects.plain: A home-built science lab for trading ideas: every idea is tested against years of market history, and only the honest survivors pass.
projects.summary: 60+ Python backtests across multi-asset OHLCV (FX majors, FX crosses, metals, indices, crypto) with pre-registered hypotheses, walk-forward out-of-sample validation, explicit bias auditing, and probabilistic Sharpe / deflated Sharpe gates. Companion literature review followed a PRISMA-style protocol across 63 IEEE papers with a multi-dimensional taxonomy.
projects.scale: 60+ backtests, PRISMA review of 63 IEEE papers
projects.deep_dive_intro: A pre-registered research framework for evaluating trading edges across many markets without fooling itself. Every claim is gated by statistical lower-bounds, every edge is tested out-of-sample on a held-out window, and every promotion to live capital requires an explicit written spec.
projects.architecture: Strategy modules under BOT/research_backtests/strategies/ each declare one family (entry, exit, sizing). A shared cost model applies broker-verified spread, commission, and slippage before any metric is computed. The runner sweeps capital and risk-per-trade grids, then computes block-bootstrap lower-bound Sharpe (SR_LB), Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio (PSR), and Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) over the trade series; promotion is gated on all three statistics jointly, with a multiple-testing haircut (exact thresholds are pre-registered internally). A separate bias auditor inspects each candidate for lookahead, same-bar fills, profit concentration, and overfit. A companion PRISMA-style literature review classifies 63 IEEE papers across a multi-dimensional taxonomy with a coverage matrix.
lessons: Sharpe-lower-bound is leverage-invariant; CAGR is leverage-illusion. Ranking by SR_LB and choosing sizing after edge selection avoided multiple tail-driven false positives that ranked top by CAGR.

A same-day daily feature is lookahead in an intraday strategy: a carry-trend candidate looked PF 2.58 pre-audit and collapsed to PF 1.00 once the daily close was lagged. The bug-class rule now lives as a sacred rule.
Broker reality beats research defaults: forcing one micro-lot fill on every symbol surfaced a $6/lot round-turn commission that the research cost model had under-estimated by 5-8x for some pairs.

A tail-driven candidate cannot be forward-validated in human timeframes: if ~89% of the edge is in the top 1.5% of campaigns, 12 forward windows give ~84% probability of a zero-tail outcome -- a useful prior to retire the family early rather than wait years.

projects.title: SURI -- Systematic literature review (IEEE, PRISMA-style)
projects.plain: I read 63 research papers on how quantum computers could one day threaten Bitcoin -- and organised everything the field knows into one clear map.
projects.summary: A pre-registered, PRISMA-style systematic mapping of quantum-computing threats to blockchain systems, organised around three research questions -- what quantum threats to Bitcoin and blockchain are studied, what defences are proposed, and how ready the ecosystem is to migrate. Sixty-three IEEE papers survive screening into the synthesis pool (from a wider identified/screened set, with non-IEEE and survey papers removed) and are coded against a multi-dimensional taxonomy and a five-category corpus grid feeding a coverage matrix. The corpus is Bitcoin-heavy and grounded in post-quantum cryptography: Shor against ECDSA, Grover against SHA-256 mining, and the NIST FIPS 203/204/205 schemes (Kyber/ML-KEM, Dilithium, SPHINCS+). Companion to the quant-research framework -- the same discipline applied to the literature side of the work.
projects.scale: 63 included papers, 3 RQs, 5-category grid, single-coder + audit pass; manuscript in preparation
projects.deep_dive_intro: SURI is a systematic mapping of the research at the intersection of blockchain security and quantum computing, run with the same operating discipline as the trading-research framework: a pre-registered protocol, a transparent search log, single-coder plus audit pass, and a coverage matrix so blind spots in the corpus fall out of the table. The manuscript is being drafted in Overleaf toward IEEE Access.
projects.architecture: A search log records every database query (IEEE Xplore under institutional access as the primary source, plus Google Scholar, arXiv, and three free standards/community sources -- NIST, IETF/CFRG, and the Bitcoin Improvement Proposals) with filters, hits, and selection reasons. PRISMA-style screening (title -> abstract -> full text) records inclusion and exclusion at every stage down to the 63 papers that enter synthesis. Each paper is placed in one of five primary corpus categories (Threat Models, PQC Constructions, Quantum-Native Designs, Hybrid Migrations, Benchmarks/Implementations) mapped onto the three research questions, and coded against a multi-dimensional taxonomy (threat type, affected target, mitigation, performance impact, privacy and usability, standards and governance). A coverage matrix renders the taxonomy as a table so thin quadrants -- for example only two threat-modelling papers against forty-five defence papers -- are visible at a glance. An idempotent Python pipeline (build -> append -> repair -> categorise -> PRISMA) regenerates the workbook and screening figure from source. Outputs: methodology, RQ map, taxonomy, coverage matrix, reference list, and search log.
projects.architecture_diagram:
IEEE Xplore + NIST     PRISMA screening        5-category grid -> 3 RQs
+-------------------+   +------------------+   +----------------------+
| search log        |-->| title screen     |-->| Threat Models  (RQ1) |
| (database + query |   | abstract screen  |   | PQC Constructions    |
|  + hits + reason) |   | full text screen |   | Quantum-Native   RQ2 |
+-------------------+   +--------+---------+   | Hybrid Migrations    |
                                 |             | Benchmarks     (RQ3) |
                                 v             +----------+-----------+
                        +--------+---------+              |
                        | 63 included      |------------->+
                        | papers           |              v
                        +------------------+   +----------+-----------+
                                               | coverage matrix      |
                                               | (multi-dim taxonomy, |
                                               |  blind-spot map)     |
                                               +----------------------+
lessons: A flat keyword list cannot reveal blind spots. A multi-dimensional taxonomy plus a coverage matrix makes an imbalance like two threat-modelling papers against forty-five defence papers fall out of the table automatically, which is the whole point of doing the review.

Search log discipline is load-bearing: without database / query / filter / hits-found / hits-selected / reason for every search, the review is not reproducible and reviewer #2 finds gaps you cannot justify.

Included is not the same as identified: the headline paper count is the synthesis pool after non-IEEE and survey papers are screened out, so the number that anchors every claim is 63, not the larger identified/screened set.

Relevance and role are separate axes. Conflating them -- the tempting extra 'Type: Core / Supporting / Context' column -- created false agreement in coding decisions and was removed after the first audit.

projects.title: Money Compass -- personal wealth aggregator
projects.plain: A private app that reads my own bank statements and shows where the money actually goes -- like a personal accountant who never sleeps.
projects.summary: A read-only personal-finance aggregator that pulls Bank of America and US credit-card transactions through the SimpleFIN Bridge and turns them into a cashflow, runway, and subscription view. It is a package inside the trading dashboard, exposed at an auth-gated /money route that fails closed and never renders financial figures on a public surface. A daily refresh task bakes the account state into a JSON snapshot so the request path never touches the bank API or the SQLite ledger directly. Phase 1 (ledger + cashflow + subscription detect) and Phase 2 (month-over-month, budget streak, goals, ranked CFO insights, spending-trend chart, savings tips, category drill-down) both ship and run live on the VPS.
projects.scale: 40+ tests, Phase 1 + Phase 2 live, auth-gated + leak-guarded
projects.deep_dive_intro: Money Compass answers one question -- where is the money going and how long does it last -- from real bank and credit-card data rather than manual entry. It is built as a package inside the existing dashboard, so it inherits the same fail-closed, no-public-money-leak discipline as the rest of the surface.
projects.architecture: A SimpleFIN read-only client fetches transactions on a daily batch (the owner claims the setup token; the code never logs in to the bank and never logs the credential). Rows land in a SQLite ledger de-duplicated by transaction id, then a categorise step runs at read time so a new rule re-labels the whole history, not just new rows -- card-to-card payments are tagged as transfers and peer transfers (Zelle) are excluded so they cannot inflate income or expense. A refresh task bakes cashflow, runway, month-over-month, budget streak, goals, ranked insights, spending history, and savings tips into data/money_summary.json via an atomic write; the /money route and /api/money-summary read that snapshot behind HTTP Basic auth. /api/money-summary is enumerated in the dashboard's MONEY_API_ROUTES leak-guard, so a test fails the build if the route is ever left un-gated.
projects.architecture_diagram:
SimpleFIN Bridge        money/ package          dashboard
+------------------+   +------------------+   +----------------+
| BofA + US cards  |-->| simplefin client |-->| /money (auth)  |
| (read-only, 1x/d)|   | store (SQLite)   |   | /api/money-... |
+------------------+   | categorise       |   +-------+--------+
                       | compass/insight  |           |
                       +--------+---------+           v
                                |             +-------+--------+
                                v             | leak-guard     |
                       money_summary.json --->| MONEY_API_...  |
                       (atomic snapshot)      | (401 if public)|
                                              +----------------+
lessons: Categorise at read time, not on insert: applying rules inside the snapshot builder means a new rule instantly re-labels the entire history, which cut uncategorised spend from thousands of dollars to a few hundred without a backfill migration.

Card-to-card payments and peer transfers are not income or expense: an autopay between two of your own accounts double-counts on both sides and Zelle looks like salary unless you carve both into an excluded-category set shared by every consumer of the snapshot.

A credential can leak through an exception, not just a log line: a raw request error carried the Basic-auth access URL out through stderr, so the client now re-raises with HTTP status only -- diagnostics never carry the URL.

A leak-guard that enumerates every /api route by name is stronger than a code-review habit: the money summary route is only trustworthy on a public-facing dashboard because a test fails the build the moment it is not in the auth-gated list.

projects.title: Edge Factory -- research-automation pipeline
projects.plain: An assembly line for research ideas: drop an idea in one end and it gets tested the same fair way every time -- most ideas die cheap, and the rare good one earns a full report.
projects.summary: A thin Python orchestrator that runs a strategy candidate down a nine-station conveyor -- seed, expand, dedup, prescreen, backtest, bias-audit, statistical gate, dossier, human verdict -- so systematic-trading ideas are evaluated the same way every time. The design point is not generating many ideas but killing bad ones cheaply and early: a factory without a hard kill-gate just produces false positives at high speed. Two safety invariants are locked in code -- the pipeline always stops at the dossier and never has a path to live capital, and no agent can approve its own candidate. The MVP wires the dedup, prescreen, and statistical gate automatically around a reused fleet of existing research tools.
projects.scale: MVP v0.1 committed, 36 pytest passing, pyright 0, forbidden-import guard 0
projects.deep_dive_intro: Edge Factory is a conveyor for trading-research candidates. Each idea enters as a bundle with an economic rationale and either dies at an early kill-gate or reaches a full dossier that a human reads before any verdict -- the machine never promotes anything on its own.
projects.architecture: A single orchestrator (edge_factory.py) sequences nine stations but builds almost nothing new: it reuses an existing prescreen, a Sharpe go/no-go gate, a CPCV/PBO overfit check, a shared backtest harness, a bias auditor, and an experiment registry. A candidate first hits a hard dedup gate against a registry of already-NULL families; survivors run prescreen, then a backtest, then the statistical gate (block-bootstrap lower-bound Sharpe, PSR, and a deflated-Sharpe haircut whose multiple-testing penalty scales with how many variants were expanded). The pipeline then writes a dossier and STOPS -- there is no code path from a GO_CANDIDATE label to live execution, and the approve command is a separate human step. Candidates killed at prescreen short-circuit before a dossier is written, so the presence or absence of a dossier tells you exactly where a family died. Every kill and verdict is appended to an experiment registry CSV.
projects.architecture_diagram:
seed -> expand -> dedup-gate -> prescreen -> backtest
                       |                          |
                   (NULL family              (bad payoff
                    KILL here)                 KILL here)
                                                  |
                                                  v
                                            bias-audit
                                                  |
                                                  v
                                     SR_LB / PSR / DSR gate
                                                  |
                                                  v
                                    +-------------+---------+
                                    | dossier = STOP        |
                                    | (no path to live)     |
                                    +-------------+---------+
                                                  |
                                                  v
                                      human verdict (approve/reject)
lessons: The scarce skill is killing, not generating: without a hard dedup gate against already-NULL families, a fast idea-generator just re-discovers the same dead edges, so the dedup step is a hard gate rather than an advisory warning.

Where a candidate dies is itself a signal: a prescreen kill short-circuits before any dossier is written while a gate rejection produces one, so the mere presence of a dossier tells you the family passed payoff sanity and failed on statistics.

The multiple-testing haircut has to scale with the search: the deflated-Sharpe penalty takes the number of expanded variants as N_trials, so a station that fans out more candidates automatically makes the gate harder to pass rather than easier.

A research pipeline needs a coded air-gap, not a policy: the dossier stage is the terminal node with no function that reaches an order path, so a GO_CANDIDATE label is a research annotation that cannot become a live trade by accident.

projects.title: Live web karaoke -- group mode
projects.plain: Turns your phone into a karaoke microphone for the TV -- nothing to install, just scan a code and sing.
projects.summary: A no-install progressive web app that turns a phone into a karaoke microphone and streams the vocal to a TV or laptop over WebRTC, with a QR-code join flow and a group party mode as the core use case. The hard engineering problem was audio latency: the singer hears their own voice through the air instantly and again from the speaker late, so the app drives the receiver's jitter buffer down to remove the browser's default 100-200ms of playout padding. It is deployed live on Vercel and stays within YouTube's terms by embedding the official iframe player rather than scraping audio. A service worker caches the shell for offline-capable reloads, with an explicit cache-version discipline after a stale-render incident.
projects.scale: Live on Vercel, v0.5.1, group-mode validation in progress
projects.deep_dive_intro: This is a phone-as-microphone karaoke app where the wedge is zero install: scan a QR code, sing into the phone, hear it on the big screen. The interesting work is all in the audio path, where WebRTC's comfort-first defaults fight against live singing.
projects.architecture: The phone captures the microphone and opens a WebRTC audio call to the TV host via PeerJS; the TV plays the incoming stream alongside the YouTube IFrame player showing the backing track. On the receiver, every audio RTCRtpReceiver has playoutDelayHint set to 0 (feature-detected -- Chromium and Edge only, a no-op elsewhere) to strip the browser's default 100-200ms jitter padding, trading a little smoothness for live monitorability; the irreducible floor (Opus codec plus one-way WiFi plus OS output buffer) remains. The app loads the YouTube IFrame API dynamically only after registering its ready callback, because a static deferred module can miss the API-ready event and hang the player. A service worker precaches the app shell, and every CSS/JS change bumps both the asset query string and the service-worker CACHE_VERSION together, or the worker serves a stale render.
projects.architecture_diagram:
phone (mic)                     TV / laptop (host)
+-------------+   WebRTC audio   +-------------------+
| getUserMedia|---------------->| RTCRtpReceiver    |
| PeerJS call |   (PeerJS)       | playoutDelayHint=0|
+-------------+                  +---------+---------+
      ^                                    |
      | QR join                            v
      |                          +---------+---------+
+-----+-------+                  | YouTube IFrame    |
| service     |                  | (backing track,   |
| worker cache|                  |  ToS-compliant)   |
+-------------+                  +-------------------+
lessons: The audio delay was not the network -- it was the browser: the dominant lag in live WebRTC audio is the receiver's default jitter/playout buffer (~100-200ms of padding for smoothness), and setting playoutDelayHint to 0 on the receiver removes it where Chromium supports the hint.

There is a physical floor you cannot code away: Opus encode/decode plus one-way WiFi plus the OS output buffer is tens of milliseconds no matter what, so a phone held in the hand always doubles its own air-path voice against the late speaker -- true monitoring belongs on the phone, not across a round trip.

A deferred ES module can lose a race with a static third-party script: loading the YouTube IFrame API from inside the module after registering the ready callback fixed a player that hung whenever the API fired before the module was live.

A service worker will happily serve yesterday's build: after a stale render, the rule became bump the asset query string and CACHE_VERSION in the same commit, because bumping only one still ships the cached copy.

projects.title: Trading Journal -- decision-intelligence layer
projects.plain: A diary that grades my own decisions: when I overrode the system by hand, did that actually help? The diary answers with numbers, not feelings.
projects.summary: A read-only decision-intelligence layer over a real-money trading track that scores whether the operator's manual closes actually beat the bot's own trailing exit, then narrates the day as a short desk note. It never touches the edge or any order path -- it only reads the realised trade log and the divergence report. The daily note is written by a Groq-hosted model as decorative prose while the numbers stay authoritative, and it is exposed at an auth-gated /journal route rendered as a desk-blotter page with a P&L calendar heatmap. Phase 1 (the deterministic scorecard) is live on the VPS with an hourly producer task.
projects.scale: Phase 1 live on VPS, 15 tests, auth-gated + metric-drift tripwire
projects.deep_dive_intro: The Trading Journal asks a narrow, honest question of a real trading track: when the operator overrode the bot and closed a position by hand, did that discretion add or subtract versus letting the bot's trail run? Everything else -- the narrative, the calendar -- hangs off that one measured number.
projects.architecture: An ingest module reads the realised trade rows and campaign metadata and reuses the existing per-campaign divergence computation; the counterfactual is the exit-slip R (realised price minus the paper exit price, per tier, in R units) rather than a naive gross-minus-paper subtraction that is identically zero by construction. A scorecard aggregates the manual-close delta with a bootstrap confidence interval and a verdict that never authorises a risk increase below a minimum sample. A producer runs on an hourly task and writes the scorecard JSON via an atomic write; a separate narrator builds a prompt and calls a Groq-hosted model to write a four-sentence Thai desk note, failing soft to a template when the model is unavailable, with the key scrubbed from any output. The dashboard loads both files fail-soft and renders /journal as a self-contained desk-blotter page -- rubber-stamp verdict, signature memo, and a month-grid P&L calendar coloured by dollar profit -- all behind HTTP Basic auth and enumerated in the money-route leak-guard.
projects.architecture_diagram:
realised.csv + divergence      e8 producers            dashboard
+----------------------+   +------------------+   +------------------+
| per-campaign         |-->| journal_ingest   |-->| /journal (auth)  |
| exit-slip R          |   | journal_scorecard|   | desk-blotter +   |
+----------------------+   +--------+---------+   | P&L calendar     |
                                    |             +--------+---------+
                                    v                      ^
                           +--------+---------+            |
                           | narrator (Groq)  |---> narrative.json
                           | fail-soft->tmpl  |     + Telegram card
                           +------------------+
lessons: The obvious counterfactual was identically zero: subtracting a paper-R that is just a relabel of the realised R always yields nothing, so the real metric is the per-tier exit-slip R already computed for the divergence report -- reuse it, never recompute it.

A verdict on a real-money track has to refuse below a minimum sample: with too few manual closes the scorecard returns INSUFFICIENT_SAMPLE and explicitly does not authorise scaling risk, which is a safety property, not a UI state.

The prose is decorative and the numbers are authoritative: the model narrates the day but a rule forbids it from quoting raw field or JSON-key names, and the note fails soft to a deterministic template so a model outage never blocks the daily card.

A cross-tree import will 502 on deploy: the producer originally imported a dashboard helper that does not exist in the live-trading tree, so it was rewritten to an inline temp-plus-replace write to keep the two deployment trees independent.

blog.tagline: Short writeups on what I am learning -- updated occasionally.

posts.title: A cost model that cannot change the answer
posts.teaser: Sharpe is scale-invariant. Multiply every trade by a near-constant factor and the ratio does not move -- so a cost model built that way can look conservative for a year and be inert the whole time.
posts.body: Here is an error worth naming, because it hid in my own pipeline for a year and it is invisible by construction. Suppose you charge costs by keeping a fraction of each trade's gross return -- net = gross * k, with k somewhere near 0.92 depending on conditions. It reads as conservative. It cannot work. If k barely varies, multiplying every observation by it is a scale transform: mean and standard deviation move together and the ratio between them does not move at all. Sharpe is scale-invariant, so no amount of tightening that percentage will change the verdict. You can set the haircut anywhere you like and the answer is the same, which should have been the tell. Costs have to be charged per position, in the units the position actually pays, at the moment it pays them -- and they have to increase the magnitude of a loss, not reduce it. That second point is its own trap: a haircut written as net = gross * k quietly makes losing trades smaller, refunding the worst outcomes, and if most of your trades lose then the sign error flatters you exactly where it hurts most. I found both faults by auditing a headline of my own against a pass/fail bar written down before I looked. The corrected figure fell under my own gate and the result was withdrawn. Two adversarial review rounds then attacked the audit, and the second attacked the first. This was not a discovery about markets. It was a discovery about my own measurement, which is the more common kind and the one nobody publishes.

posts.title: The file drawer is the finding
posts.teaser: Hou, Xue and Zhang found 65% of published anomalies fail a t>1.96 hurdle. Franco and co-authors found 10 of 48 null results reach print. The nulls are the part nobody ships.
posts.body: Over fifteen months I ran 81 strategy studies in roughly twenty families, each scored by a rule fixed before the test. Most were rejected. Publishing that is unusual in practice but it is exactly what the finance literature has been asking for. Harvey, Liu and Zhu showed that with hundreds of published factors a t-statistic of 2.0 means little and the hurdle sits nearer 3.0. Hou, Xue and Zhang found 65% of 452 anomalies fail even at 1.96. Franco, Malhotra and Simonovits measured the file drawer directly: 10 of 48 null results reached print against 56 of 91 strong ones. The Journal of Corporate Finance gave a 2025 special issue to statistically non-significant results for the same reason. Bailey and Lopez de Prado make the point sharpest -- the deflated Sharpe haircut is a function of how many configurations you tried, so a Sharpe is uninterpretable unless the trial count is known. A registry of rejections is how that denominator becomes honest. The counter-case deserves airtime too: Jensen, Kelly and Pedersen argue most factors do replicate under a Bayesian hierarchy, and I cannot adjudicate that from one lab. What I can do is publish my denominator.

posts.title: PSR / DSR -- why CAGR lies under leverage
posts.teaser: Sharpe is leverage-invariant; CAGR is not. A 1000% backtest hides nothing more than a 100% one with 10x leverage.
posts.body: Across a quarter of research I kept ranking strategies by CAGR and kept being surprised when 'better' systems drew down more. The mistake is well-documented but worth re-deriving: under a fixed strategy, position-sizing by a factor L scales both CAGR and max drawdown ~linearly. So Sharpe (return / standard deviation) is invariant to L while CAGR is not. The corollary -- if I pick the highest-CAGR config without locking risk first, I am choosing the most leveraged version of an indeterminate edge. The fix is a single-line discipline: select by block-bootstrap lower-bound Sharpe, then choose the smallest risk_pct that meets the target. PSR (Probabilistic Sharpe) further accounts for skew + kurtosis; DSR (Deflated Sharpe) bolts on a multiple-testing haircut for the best-of-N search. With these two gates documented, the equity-curve nostalgia stops mattering.

posts.title: Subagent-driven development -- two-stage review caught 80% of defects
posts.teaser: Across 14 SDD cycles on /portfolio v1.0-v1.4, every commit went through implementer + spec-compliance + code-quality reviewer. Hit rate was higher than self-review.
posts.body: The pattern is simple. Each task in the implementation plan gets THREE subagent runs: (1) an implementer who writes the code + appends tests, (2) a spec-compliance reviewer who confirms the code matches the plan verbatim or justifies deviation, (3) a code-quality reviewer who looks for defects the implementer missed. The implementer commits; the reviewers do NOT mutate code, only emit reports. Across 14 review cycles on this portfolio project, 8 ended with REQUEST_CHANGES or APPROVE_WITH_NITS that surfaced real bugs (listener leaks, cache poisoning on non-200, off-by-one in 365d cap, ambiguous test assertions, dead variables). Self-review by the implementer caught maybe 30% of these. Two-stage review caught the rest. The cost is real -- each task is 3x the LLM tokens of just-write-it -- but the defect-escape rate is low enough that I now treat it as the default for non-trivial work.

posts.title: Building /portfolio v1.0 -> v1.4 in 24 commits over one weekend
posts.teaser: Day 1: parchment editorial page. Day 2: IDE Inspector redesign. Day 3: multi-page split + polish. Day 4: audience-specific routes. The arc.
posts.body: v1 was a single editorial page on Saturday: parchment background, serif body, KM avatar. It worked but felt indistinguishable from any other student portfolio. v1.1 was the IDE Inspector redesign: title bar + file tree + tabs + status bar, with five wow features (keyboard cheat sheet, commit-activity grid, view-source modal, print stylesheet, now-playing status). v1.2 was the multi-page split -- one 6000-pixel scroll became five routes with proper navigation. v1.3 added per-project deep-dives + SVG illustrations + the latest.md gap-closer. v1.4 added the two audience-specific share URLs (/grad-school + /recruit) for recruiters and grad-school admissions readers. Each version: spec doc + implementation plan + SDD task-by-task + push + deploy. The deploy script had to learn three lessons the hard way -- PS5.1 redirects on native exes are fatal, scp does not glob, and new static subdirs need explicit ship rules.

posts.title: Honest numbers only -- prop-firm $-figures stay out of public pages
posts.teaser: Test test_route_portfolio_no_pnl_numbers regexes the rendered HTML for dollar-digit patterns and fails the build if anything leaks.
posts.body: Prop-firm rules forbid posting account balances and P&L figures in public. The portfolio page is public. So a single test sits in test_portfolio.py and regexes the rendered HTML across all 10 routes for any dollar-prefixed digit substring. If anything matches -- a stray account-size mention from a Now-Playing status, a per-month figure in a project summary, a per-lot commission figure -- the test fails the build. It has fired twice in this codebase (once during F5 Now Playing implementation, once during a project-summary edit). Each time the fix was to rephrase without the figure. The rule is fail-loud in CI, not policed by code review. That is the right level of automation for a prop-firm-adjacent public surface.

posts.title: Fail-closed by default -- a 503 beats a wrong page
posts.teaser: Every route on this dashboard returns 503 on schema invalidity rather than rendering a partial page. The bug class it prevents is worse than downtime.
posts.body: When a JSON config goes bad -- a missing key, a corrupted file, a typo -- the wrong response is to render a half-page with defaults. The right response is to return 503 and surface the underlying error. The /portfolio loader validates required keys before any render and raises PortfolioContentError, which the route maps to a 503 with the message body. Same pattern lives in /projects (fail-closed on schema invalidity) and /anchor (fail-closed on missing rules file). Cost: rare false-positive outages when a deploy ships a malformed file. Benefit: never a silent page-rendered-but-wrong incident. Tests assert the 503 path with a monkey-patched bad source: if a future refactor swallows the error and renders a stub, the test fires. The whole approach is uglier on the happy path and stronger on the unhappy one -- which is the right tradeoff for a public surface that a recruiter or admissions reader might be looking at right now.

null_registry.headline: A registry of everything that did not work
null_registry.tagline: 81 strategy studies, scored by one decision rule that was fixed before each test and never adjusted after it. 71 rejected, 4 inconclusive, 6 blocked. A further 8 lanes never became studies at all.

status_notice.label: Draft. Partially validated.
status_notice.body: Both layers have now been controlled and both results are below. The statistics do not manufacture edges from noise but are far less sensitive than the threshold suggests. The engine has three confirmed defects -- all optimistic, all named below. Because every family here was rejected, an optimistic engine makes those rejections firmer rather than weaker; it is the survivors and the inconclusive rows that it cannot vouch for. Figures in the table are transcribed from an internal research log rather than regenerated from source. Treat every row as provisional.

protocol.intro: Every family below was scored by the same decision rule, committed to before that family was tested.

rules.name: Zero-cost lower bound
rules.body: A block-bootstrap 5th-percentile Sharpe taken before any cost model is applied. Below 1.00 there is no edge for costs to erode, and no filter, window or overlay recovers it.

rules.name: Probabilistic Sharpe
rules.body: PSR at or above 0.95, which prices skew and kurtosis instead of assuming returns are normal.

rules.name: Deflated Sharpe
rules.body: DSR at or above 0.95 with the number of trials declared, so a best-of-N search pays a multiple-testing haircut.

rules.name: Drawdown cap
rules.body: Bootstrapped 95th-percentile drawdown must sit inside a cap written down before the test, at the sizing chosen.

rules.name: Costs first
rules.body: Measured spread and slippage enter before any statistic is computed, never as an afterwards adjustment.

protocol.note: Selection is by Sharpe lower bound, never by CAGR. Position sizing scales return and drawdown together, so ranking by CAGR selects the most leveraged version of an undetermined edge.

instrument.headline: Does the gate actually measure?
instrument.intro: A registry of rejections is only evidence if the instrument that produced them can discriminate. A gate that rejects everything writes the same table as a gate that works. So the gate was given synthetic return series whose true Sharpe was fixed by construction, and asked to judge them. Each cell is the share of 100 independent draws that cleared all three thresholds.
findings: Specificity holds. On pure noise -- a true Sharpe of exactly zero -- the gate passed 0% of draws. It does not invent edges, so the rejections in the table below are not an artefact of a gate firing at random.

Sensitivity is much weaker than the threshold implies. The gate needs a true annualised Sharpe of about 2.5 before it passes more often than not on four years of daily data. At a true Sharpe of 1.5 -- a strategy most desks would run -- it passes 14% of the time. On one year of data it does not reach a coin flip even at a true Sharpe of 3.0.

So most rows below sit under the detection floor. They record that no effect large enough for this instrument to see was present at that sample size. They do not establish that no effect exists, and the summary phrase I had been using internally -- that the tractable search space was exhausted -- claims more than this evidence supports.
Scope: the above controls the statistics layer -- the lower-bound Sharpe, PSR and deflated-Sharpe estimators and their thresholds, imported unchanged. The engine layer is covered separately, below.

engine.headline: And does the engine fill and cost correctly?
engine.intro: The statistics can be right while the simulator underneath is wrong, so the fill, cost and lookahead paths were put through the same treatment: bars constructed so the correct answer is arithmetic. 9 of 12 cases pass. 3 do not, and they are named here rather than left for a reader to discover.

failures.name: A stop on a gapped bar fills at the stop price
failures.detail: Given a bar that opens well beyond the stop, the simulator still books the stop level. The real fill is the open, so the loss is understated -- in the control fixture, -1R reported against -4R actual.

failures.name: The entry bar is never scanned for stops
failures.detail: A trade whose own entry bar trades through the stop is not closed there; it survives to later bars. Trades that should have died immediately are given a second chance.

failures.name: Resampling pulls in one bar of the future
failures.detail: Rows are indexed by bar open time, but the resampler labels right and closes right, so the aggregated bar labelled T includes the sub-bar that opens at T. Any study that resampled to a higher timeframe saw one sub-bar it should not have.

reading: All three lean the same way: they make results look better than they were. Losses are understated, doomed trades survive, and a sliver of future information is visible.

That direction matters for how this page should be read. Every family in the table below was REJECTED under those defects. Correcting them can only push a result down, so a rejection stands -- if anything it becomes firmer. The nulls survive their own engine's bugs.

What the defects can manufacture is the opposite outcome. The two survivors and the four inconclusive entries are exactly the rows an optimistic fill could have produced, and this control does not clear them. They are not claimed as validated anywhere on this page, and that is why.

Cost accounting passed on all three checks: the charge matches the declared model, it makes a losing trade worse rather than better, and it scales inversely with stop distance instead of behaving like a constant fraction. The cost defect found by an earlier audit is not present on this path.

families.lesson: No edge existed even gross of costs, so the failure is in the ranking hypothesis rather than in execution or fees.

families.name: Cross-asset lead-lag propagation
families.lesson: A genuinely weak but real signal still dies once the deflated Sharpe ratio charges for the number of trials that produced it.

families.name: Cross-sectional momentum / carry / time-series momentum sleeve hunt
families.lesson: Volatility targeting, cluster collapse and a multi-market trend book were all rejected together, closing the sleeve concept rather than any single construction.

families.name: Behavioural panic reversion (oscillator extremes)
families.lesson: The more extreme the panic threshold the worse the result, consistent with Nagel (2012), in which panic is a liquidity-provision premium paid by the impatient taker rather than a reversion opportunity.

families.name: Volatility clustering / compression breakout
families.lesson: Volatility clustering predicts magnitude, not direction, so a compression signal can be statistically real and still carry zero tradeable information.

families.name: Commitment-of-traders positioning follow / fade
families.lesson: Following large speculative positioning was strongly negative while fading it was mildly positive, so the directional prior was inverted and the surviving version was still not tradeable net of costs.

families.name: Overnight / night-session return premium
families.lesson: The data source synthesises each daily open from the prior close, so there is no true session gap to measure -- this is a data limitation, not a falsified hypothesis.

families.name: Pre-scheduled-event drift (rate decisions, inflation and payroll prints)
families.lesson: A timezone handling bug initially produced a false null, so the negative result was only trustworthy after the clock alignment was fixed and the test rerun.

families.name: Variance-risk-premium regime conditioning on indices
families.lesson: Using an implied-volatility measure as a conditioner produced no directional edge at the daily horizon, confirming that regime filters select conditions but do not create direction.

families.name: Momentum recipe expanded to 29 markets
families.asset_scope: Indices, metals, energy, FX, crypto -- H4
families.lesson: All three full-sample lenses (zero-cost Sharpe, deflated Sharpe, portfolio delta) were fooled at once and only an out-of-sample long/short decomposition exposed the equity indices as bull-market beta, with short-side lower bounds far below zero.

families.name: Most-popular charting indicators, broad symbol sweep
families.asset_scope: BTC + 35 instruments -- D1 (crypto, FX, index, metal, energy)
families.z0_display: 105 cells, zero go; best trend variant 1.90 annualised collapses to SR_LB 0.47
families.lesson: Every popular indicator is derived from the same price series, so a new indicator is a new formula over old information and cannot be a new edge -- one candidate passed both the probabilistic and deflated Sharpe screens and was only killed by the long/short beta decomposition.

families.name: Faithful replication of a published trend indicator on gold
families.lesson: The advertised profit factor was computed with no commission, no slippage and no stop declared, and the charting platform silently truncated the sample to the most recent bull window, so the headline was a zero-cost result on a cherry-picked span; the strategy also lost to simply holding the asset.

families.name: Free on-chain directional signals (valuation ratio, activity, exchange netflow)
families.z0_display: best 0.49 (netflow 7d MA), all 20 variants below gate
families.lesson: On a single asset with a large secular uptrend every long signal is beta and every short signal loses, so a two-sided statistical edge is nearly impossible to isolate without a cross-section.

families.name: Cross-sectional on-chain activity, market-neutral
families.z0_display: best +0.112 (and that was the price-momentum control, not an on-chain signal)
families.lesson: Removing market beta by construction did not reveal a hidden signal -- every genuine on-chain feature was negative -- which rules out beta contamination as the explanation for the earlier directional null.

families.name: Paid on-chain and derivatives-positioning comprehensive sweep
families.z0_display: 0 survivors; best blind alpha below the noise benchmark for the number of trials
families.lesson: A blind sweep of nearly eight thousand combinations must be scored against the best result luck alone would produce at that trial count, and the one signal with a directional prior turned out to be a recent-regime artifact that vanished when the last four months were removed.

families.name: Prior-day high/low barrier targeting
families.lesson: Hit probability matched the random-walk prediction to the bucket across tens of thousands of cases, and the apparently attractive raw currency P&L was pure heteroskedastic beta that inverted once returns were expressed in risk units and block-bootstrapped.

families.name: Manipulation-candle fib fade on an index proxy, V1+V2
families.z0_display: V1 negative everywhere; V2 passed every gate but was an artifact
families.lesson: A configuration passing every quantitative gate with a Sharpe above 10 and a 98% win rate was a phantom-stop artifact -- the stop sat almost six times farther away than the target and was essentially never touched, so returns were being divided by risk the position never actually took; an intraday Sharpe above 2.5 with a win rate above 98% is a red flag, and the target/stop hit rates and distance ratio must be inspected directly.

families.name: Turn-of-the-month pension-flow effect on a broad equity index
families.lesson: The effect was clearly present in the training era and collapsed in the test era with a decade-by-decade decay, which is the post-publication arbitrage decay documented by McLean and Pontiff (2016) and shows that identifying a real forced-flow counterparty is necessary but not sufficient.

families.name: Calendar and seasonal anomaly batch (day-of-week, holiday, expiry-week, sell-in-May, year-end)
families.asset_scope: US equity index ETF -- D1, 1993-2026 (8419 days)
families.lesson: Batching an entire published-anomaly lane into one screen with a reproducing anchor validates the screen and closes the lane at once; zero-cost scoring makes the null conservative because costs can only worsen it.

families.name: Ratio momentum / relative-strength spread, dollar-neutral
families.lesson: The hypothesis that a price ratio escapes bull beta failed because the small profit came entirely from one leg outperforming, and the short-ratio side was negative, so the result was one-sided drift rather than two-sided alpha.

families.name: Betting-against-beta / cross-sectional low volatility
families.asset_scope: 17 mixed instruments -- D1 (FX, indices, commodities, crypto)
families.lesson: The leverage-constraint anomaly of Frazzini and Pedersen (2014) needs a full equity cross-section with real margin structure to exist; on a seventeen-instrument mixed-class slice the premium inverted, and within-class tests confirmed it was not merely a cross-class artifact.

families.name: Turn-of-month calendar on a multi-asset basket
families.lesson: Demeaning positions removed the entire apparent premium, exposing it as market beta, and the strongly positive raw P&L and profit factor sat alongside a negative risk-adjusted lower bound -- precisely why the gate is defined on the bootstrapped lower bound and not on P&L.

families.name: Full back-test of one retail education channel's indicator systems
families.asset_scope: Three FX majors -- H1 and H4, 2024-2026
families.lesson: Claimed win rates of 73-75% measured at 34-42%, and the one near-positive system was a small-sample single-currency carry artifact that inverted between training and test -- the episode motivated adding a vendor smell-test (published Sharpe, total pips, worst drawdown, sibling products) ahead of any back-test.

families.name: Breakout with support/resistance retest, fixed 1:1 target
families.z0_display: not run -- killed by payoff arithmetic
families.lesson: A fixed 1:1 reward-to-risk structure requires better than a 50% hit rate merely to break even before costs and roughly 55% after spread, so the arithmetic alone kills it without spending a back-test.

families.name: Full smart-money cascade at H4 (bias, sweep, displacement, gap entry, liquidity target)
families.lesson: Raising the timeframe to reduce cost cannot rescue a family whose zero-cost signal already collapses out-of-sample, because the zero-cost reading contains no cost to remove.

families.name: Multi-timeframe alignment stack with 2:1 target
families.lesson: Fixing a bad exit ratio cannot help when the entry carries no signal: requiring five timeframes to agree is a trend filter, and on a rising metal that is beta, which the long/short split exposed immediately.

families.name: FX cross-sectional interest-rate carry
families.lesson: Three implementation bugs each moved the answer materially -- omitting the carry accrual itself, an unbounded inverse-volatility weight that caused return explosions, and holiday gap bars producing impossible single-day moves -- so the premium can only be judged after the accounting is right, and even then it was two-sided but statistically flat, consistent with the post-crisis decay documented in the literature.

families.name: FX cross-sectional value / purchasing-power-parity reversion
families.z0_display: best -0.185, all 8 cells -0.19 to -0.33; out-of-sample -0.86 to -1.18
families.lesson: Value and momentum are structurally opposed, and in a trend-dominated sample the currency that looks persistently cheap keeps weakening -- which is the same reason a momentum construction survived screening where a value construction did not.

families.name: Hour-of-week seasonality with mean-reversion in quiet windows
families.lesson: The quiet-window premise was confirmed statistically (bucket activity ranks persisted across train and test with rank correlation 0.60) yet produced no payoff, because low activity lowers variance without creating direction.

families.name: Volatility term-structure carry / short-volatility timing
families.z0_display: +0.454 and +0.027; net out-of-sample negative in every cell
families.lesson: The signal behaved exactly as theory predicts and still failed, because the term structure is in the profitable state roughly 92% of the time, so a binary rule is almost always on and is therefore indistinguishable from static exposure -- the beta guard (does it beat always-on?) is what separates a timing alpha from a risk premium.

families.name: Naive copying of legislator stock disclosures
families.z0_display: median excess -0.51% at 90d / -0.58% at 180d; beats benchmark 47.6% of the time
families.lesson: Published copy-trading results measure from the transaction date, which only the original trader can access, whereas a copier can only enter after the disclosure lag -- and a positive mean alongside a below-coin-flip hit rate signals a few right-skewed winners rather than a book-wide edge.

families.name: Government-bond auction supply pressure (dealer inventory concession)
families.asset_scope: Long-bond ETF and note future -- daily, 2002-2026 (434 auctions)
families.lesson: The real basis-point concession documented by Lou, Yan and Zhang (2013) can be undetectable through an aggregate long-duration vehicle, and a central bank acting as a dominant buyer for much of the sample absorbs exactly the concession the trade was designed to harvest.

families.name: Post-news impulse momentum continuation
families.asset_scope: Gold M1 (3 years) and EURUSD M1 (4.4 years)
families.lesson: Price mean-reverts rather than continues after a spike, both directions lost, and crucially the news-window result was statistically indistinguishable from the non-news window -- knowing when a release lands is worthless when the move depends on the surprise, whose sign is unknowable in advance.

families.name: Hour-of-day and session-window directional scan (European session)
families.z0_display: session buckets -0.16 to -1.57; two teasing buckets +1.20 / +1.08 before costs
families.lesson: The two buckets that passed were a single-regime currency-bear beta that inverted in later years and died against a sub-basis-point cost, and an adversarial review of the scanner itself found a session-open gap leak, selection contamination and a daylight-saving misalignment that invalidated the fixed-window cells.

families.name: Asia-session edge archetype scan
families.z0_display: 13 of 16 archetypes were duplicates of already-closed families
families.lesson: Screening a whole session's worth of ideas against the closed-family registry before touching data eliminated 13 of 16 candidates for free, leaving only one with a genuine forced-flow counterparty to actually test.

families.name: Index M5 trend-pullback at swing levels
families.lesson: Win rates landed on the coin-flip breakeven for each reward ratio almost exactly (49.9% against 50%, 34.8% against 33.3%), which is the signature of a random entry and shows the swing-level pullback adds nothing.

families.name: Tokyo morning fixing-flow (five-and-ten day effect)
families.lesson: A pre-registered early/late sample split killed it cleanly -- positive in the early half, sharply negative in the recent half -- and a placebo on non-fixing days matched or beat the real signal, proving the drift was currency beta and not the fixing flow.

families.name: Insider cluster-buy post-filing drift
families.lesson: Conviction slices got monotonically worse as the number of participating insiders rose, which is the signature of no signal (a real edge strengthens with conviction), and the portfolio-level lower bound of 0.70 came from diversification rather than per-event signal quality, which was approximately zero.

families.name: Leveraged-ETF end-of-day rebalance flow
families.asset_scope: Two US index ETFs -- 1-min, 251 trading days
families.lesson: The forced-flow mechanism was genuinely visible in the data (two-sided continuation concentrated on high-volatility days, exactly as Cheng and Madhavan (2009) describe) and still failed on three independent walls: the profit came from a handful of tail days so the bootstrapped lower bound was negative, the gross edge per day was smaller than round-trip cost, and the venue we can actually trade offers neither the instrument nor the closing auction the edge lives in.

families.name: Post-earnings-announcement drift (analyst-surprise definition)
families.z0_display: long +1.39% abnormal at 63d, t=5.40; crude Sharpe 0.71-0.87
families.lesson: The only long side in dozens of probes that was not null, but the short leg was dead and the free data covers only surviving companies, so the honest ceiling is well below the gate and resolving it requires point-in-time survivorship-free data.

families.name: Post-earnings drift, seasonal-random-walk (standardised unexpected earnings) definition
families.z0_display: long +0.79% at 63d, t=2.01; long-short not significant at any horizon
families.lesson: Deciding whether to buy data is itself a testable question: the affordable survivorship-free vendor carries no analyst estimates, so it could only ever measure the weaker seasonal-random-walk definition of Foster, Olsen and Shevlin (1984) and Bernard and Thomas (1989), and the middle quintile outperformed the top one -- non-monotonic response is the same no-signal signature seen in the insider-conviction work.

families.name: Daily short-volume ratio (order-flow proxy)
families.z0_display: high-ratio -0.27% abnormal at 21d, t=-2.18; long-short t=1.12 not significant
families.lesson: Short volume is a flow measure and not the short-interest position measure used by Diether, Lee and Werner (2009); the informed-short direction was correct but one-sided and smaller than the borrow fee, so it is real yet not tradeable.

families.name: Month-end benchmark-fix rebalancing drift
families.z0_display: full-sample t=-2.10 collapses to t=+0.29 out-of-sample
families.lesson: With roughly 47 events the test of the Melvin and Prins (2015) rebalancing flow was underpowered by construction, and the one strong full-sample reading was an in-sample trend artifact -- the regulatory widening of the fixing window plus bank and high-frequency arbitrage removed whatever was left.

families.name: Post-macro-event daily drift (1-3 day hold)
families.asset_scope: US equity index ETF -- D1, 2015-2026 (219 events)
families.z0_display: all horizons t=-0.96 to -1.31, continuation rate 44-47%
families.lesson: The mean was negative rather than merely insignificant, matching the intraday post-news result that price reverts after events; an audit also caught a cost-sign inversion that had been fabricating a positive short leg.

families.name: Dealer quoted-spread dynamics as a signal (not as a cost)
families.lesson: Switching the decisive read from Sharpe to information coefficient turned a soft null into a permanent closure: an IC of 0.016 with this breadth implies an information-ratio ceiling near 0.3, so no construction, universe or timeframe could reach the gate -- and quoted spread on equity indices turns out to be a clock (time-of-day explains up to 66% of its variance) rather than the adverse-selection gauge of Glosten and Milgrom, so failing to de-seasonalise would have relabelled a closed time-of-day family as a new edge.

families.name: Path-geometry statistics (irreversibility, signature area, tail asymmetry, self-excitation, topology, ordinal patterns, curvature, excursions)
families.z0_display: 0/10 equations, all 30 measurements empty; best information-ratio ceiling 0.912
families.lesson: Measuring the raw signal's rank information coefficient before writing any trading rule is what finally closed a lane that had been reopened three times, because an optimistic ceiling below 1.0 (the Grinold fundamental-law bound) proves no rule construction could reach the gate; three measurement lessons came with it -- time-series hypotheses must be scored pooled rather than cross-sectionally (the sign can flip), a truncation-based causality probe cannot detect a backfilled warm-up leak so a perturbation probe with a negative control is required, and breadth must be counted on the holding clock.

families.name: Gaussian / normal-distribution baseline controls
families.asset_scope: 4 crypto -- H4 (same universe as the path-geometry round)
families.z0_display: 3 cost-eaten, 1 empty; measured round-turn cost 28.84 bps
families.lesson: Running known-null baselines as controls exposed a hole in the screen itself -- the information-ratio ceiling is a gross number, so the gate was blind to cost and rated a closed mean-reversion family as a pass -- and a skip-a-bar discriminator in the sense of Roll (1984) showed roughly 80% of the one-bar signal was bid-ask bounce; measured cost was six times the intuitive guess, so cost must be read from the data, never estimated mentally.

families.name: Classic candlestick patterns (fifteen named formations)
families.asset_scope: BTC and gold -- H4 and D1, 10 years
families.z0_display: 0/180 pass the gate; best SR_LB 0.50; rank IC empty in all 6 measurements
families.lesson: Cost was ruled out as the excuse because the cheapest instrument (0.57 bps round turn) failed identically, the short side was negative in all twelve slots while the long side was positive (textbook beta), and a drift-adjusted edge column showed the best-looking pattern actually underperformed doing nothing; separately, seven of fifteen patterns require an overnight gap that a 24/7 contract never produces, so most cells were structurally unmeasurable.

families.name: Value-area (VAH/VAL) fade in the first fifteen minutes
families.asset_scope: US index ETF 1-min and NAS100 3-year multi-year validation
families.z0_display: fade gross -0.151R (Sharpe -2.62); continuation -0.020R (coin flip); reject-only variant SR_LB -1.02
families.lesson: Changing the exit to a trailing stop flipped the result from strongly negative to apparently excellent, but a random-direction control with the same trailing exit scored nearly as well, showing about two-thirds of the improvement was an exit-management artifact rather than an entry edge -- and the one promising variant on a single year inverted on a three-year multi-market re-test.

families.name: Second-resolution trailing-stop scalp with continuous re-entry
families.asset_scope: BTC -- M1, one month (34k bars), observed spread
families.z0_display: gross edge positive, net deeply negative in every configuration
families.lesson: A small but genuine micro-momentum edge existed gross and was roughly one third of the round-trip cost, and cost-sensitivity was decisive: even cutting the spread to a quarter of the observed level left it losing, so the conclusion is structural rather than an artifact of the cost assumption.

families.name: Diversified futures time-series momentum, built to CTA standard
families.lesson: Building the Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen (2012) construction properly (volatility-targeted risk parity with a portfolio-level overlay) rather than porting a raw recipe reproduced the industry trend benchmark almost exactly, which is the point: retail momentum on futures earns beta at benchmark level, and dropping equities from the book collapsed the result.

families.name: Cross-sectional momentum on the same futures universe, dollar-neutral
families.z0_display: best -0.32 net / -0.25 zero-cost, all 8 cells negative
families.lesson: A measured market beta of 0.002 confirms the neutrality was real, so this is a clean absence of relative-strength alpha rather than a beta artifact -- pairing the directional and neutral variants closes the momentum-on-futures question in both directions at once.

families.name: Volatility-regime directional conditioning
families.z0_display: calendar slice test -1.88; direct low-realised-volatility gate test -2.14
families.lesson: Two independent ways of selecting the same quiet conditions both failed, confirming the general principle that a filter can select conditions but cannot create direction.

families.name: swap-rate/rollover rates as a free commodity-curve proxy
families.asset_scope: Energy, metals and crypto -- daily snapshots, 72 days
families.z0_display: not measurable -- signal updates roughly monthly
families.lesson: The proxy fails on cadence, not on concept: energy swap rates move as a step function about once a month (steps account for over 98% of all movement, with plateaus of 25-31 days), so even eighteen months of collection would yield far too few independent observations, while a contrast control on metals confirmed the collector itself was healthy and crypto swap rates were a constant markup carrying no information at all.

families.name: Cash-deal merger-arbitrage spread convergence
families.lesson: A survivorship-free deal universe is the whole test -- free sources drop delisted targets and provide no failed-deal list, so the available sample is biased toward completed deals and below the pre-registered minimum deal count.

families.name: Closed-end-fund discount-to-NAV mean reversion
families.lesson: Prices were obtainable for most of the universe but net asset value was not, and the signal is defined as the difference between them, so the engine was completed and parked pending a NAV feed rather than run on a proxy.

families.name: Options dealer-gamma exposure positioning
families.lesson: Historical open-interest by strike is not available free and cannot be backfilled, so the only free path is a forward snapshot collector whose earliest usable read is roughly two years out; the structural concern is that crypto options notional is small relative to perpetuals, so the dealer-hedging channel may be swamped.

families.name: Crypto perpetual funding carry
families.lesson: Exchange endpoints are geographically restricted or offer only a few months of history, so the hypothesis remains untested rather than falsified -- it must not be recorded as a null.

families.name: Commodity term-structure carry
families.z0_display: not measurable on current free history
families.lesson: The one free source with genuine individual contract months ends in 1999, so it can only cover the era before the anomaly decayed and carries no decision value for today.

families.name: Order-flow / true microstructure
families.asset_scope: All instruments on the available feed
families.lesson: The feed reports zero real volume on every file, so anything requiring genuine traded volume or order flow is structurally impossible on this data rather than untried.

null_registry.table_note: z0 SR_LB is the zero-cost Sharpe lower bound, the reading taken before costs. A family below 1.00 there was rejected without a cost model being run. INCONCLUSIVE marks a positive reading that did not survive out-of-sample testing or a sample too thin to score.
null_registry.blocked_intro: These lanes were closed without a verdict. Recording why a question could not be asked is part of the record.

blocked_lanes.name: Order-flow and true microstructure
blocked_lanes.reason: The available price feed reports zero real volume on every instrument, so volume-based and order-flow constructions cannot be computed at all.

blocked_lanes.name: Crypto perpetual funding carry
blocked_lanes.reason: Funding-history endpoints are either geographically blocked or expose only a few months of history; a paid or differently hosted feed would be required.

blocked_lanes.name: Options dealer-gamma positioning
blocked_lanes.reason: Historical open-interest by strike is not published free and cannot be backfilled; free dashboards show current state only. A forward-only snapshot collector is running, with the earliest usable sample roughly two years away.

blocked_lanes.name: Commodity term-structure carry (current curve)
blocked_lanes.reason: The only free source with individual contract months stops at 1999; recent curve data requires a paid or key-registered feed. A free swap-rate proxy was measured and rejected on update cadence.

blocked_lanes.name: Merger-arbitrage deal universe
blocked_lanes.reason: Free sources drop delisted targets and publish no failed-deal list, so a survivorship-free universe -- the core requirement of the test -- cannot be assembled.

blocked_lanes.name: Closed-end-fund net asset values
blocked_lanes.reason: Prices are freely available but the NAV series needed to compute the discount is not scrapable; the signal is undefined without it.

blocked_lanes.name: Point-in-time survivorship-free equity fundamentals with analyst estimates
blocked_lanes.reason: The affordable survivorship-free products carry no analyst estimate history, and the products that do are enterprise-tier; this blocks a clean re-test of the one equity event study whose long side was not null.

blocked_lanes.name: Full-cycle paid on-chain and derivatives history
blocked_lanes.reason: The accessible subscription tier covers a single bear regime of about one year; multi-cycle history sits behind a higher tier that was judged not worth buying given the one-year result.

null_registry.surviving_intro: Two families were not rejected. They are listed because a registry that publishes only its failures and quietly keeps its survivors is the selection bias this page exists to argue against. Neither is a claim: no performance figure is reported for either.

surviving.name: Momentum / herding
surviving.status: The one family this gate did not reject. Its previously published headline statistics were withdrawn on an internal cost audit and are not restated here. It is not claimed as validated, and no performance figure is reported.

surviving.name: Post-earnings-announcement drift (analyst-surprise definition)
surviving.status: Not closed, not validated. On free data the long side remained statistically significant; the short side did not.

limits: That these families do not work anywhere. Each row is a scoped claim: this construction, on these instruments, over this sample window, under this cost stack, did not clear this gate. A counterexample built differently does not contradict it.

That an absent effect is the same as an undetectable one. The control above puts this gate's detection floor near a true annualised Sharpe of 2.5 on four years of daily data. Any real edge weaker than that would have been rejected here too, so most of these rows are silence rather than absence.

That the engine is correct. It is not: three defects are confirmed and described above. They bias optimistically, which is why the rejections still stand, but a page listing rows produced by a simulator with known bugs should say so plainly rather than let a reader assume otherwise.
That the samples are long. Several families were tested on the longest history obtainable for that instrument, which is sometimes short enough that the bootstrap interval is wide.
Any claim about what is tradeable. This is backtest research on historical price data. Nothing here is a recommendation, and no result on this page should be read as one.
null_registry.falsification: If the positive control fails, this page is withdrawn rather than defended. If any family listed here is later shown to clear the gate under a corrected implementation, that entry is retracted in place, dated, with the original text left visible rather than deleted.
